'''''Acacia melanoxylon''''', commonly known as the '''Australian blackwood''', is an ''[[Acacia]]'' [[species]] native to south-eastern [[Australia]] and an invasive species in other regions of the globe. The species is also known as '''blackwood''', '''hickory''', '''mudgerabah''', '''Tasmanian blackwood''', or '''blackwood acacia'''. The tree belongs to the ''Plurinerves'' section of ''Acacia'' and is one of the most wide-ranging tree species in eastern Australia and is quite variable mostly in the size and shape of the [[Phyllode|phyllodes]].<ref name=www>{{cite web|url=http://worldwidewattle.com/infogallery/utilisation/acaciasearch/pdf/melanoxylon.pdf|title=''Acacia melanoxylon'' R. Br.|access-date=12 December 2020|work=World Wide Wattle|publisher=[[Western Australian Herbarium]]|archive-date=2 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221202102543/http://worldwidewattle.com/infogallery/utilisation/acaciasearch/pdf/melanoxylon.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:BlackwoodAcaciaPhyllode2.png|thumb|[[Phyllode]] and leaf on a young ''A. melanoxylon'' specimen. ]]
''A. melanoxylon'' is able to grow to a height of around {{cvt|20|m}} and has a [[Trunk (botany)|bole]] that is approximately {{cvt|150|cm}} in diameter. It has deeply fissured, dark-grey to black coloured bark that appears quite scaly on older trees. It has angular and ribbed branches. The bark on older trunks is dark greyish-black in colour, deeply fissured and somewhat scaly. Younger branches are [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]], ribbed and angular to flattened near the greenish coloured tips. The stems of younger plants are occasionally hairy. Like most species of ''Acacia'', adult plants have [[phyllode]]s rather than true leaves. The glabrous, glossy, leathery, dark green to greyish-green phyllodes have a length of {{cvt|4|to|16|cm}} and a width of {{cvt|6|to|30|mm}} with a variable shape. They most often have a narrowly elliptic to lanceolate shape and are straight to slightly curved and often taper near the base and have three to five prominent longitudinal veins.<ref name=lucid>{{cite web|url=https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/eafrinet/weeds/key/weeds/Media/Html/Acacia_melanoxylon_(Australian_Blackwood).htm|title=''Acacia melanoxylon'' (Australian Blackwood)|access-date=12 December 2020|work=Keys and Fact sheets|publisher=Bionet|year=2011}}</ref>

In its native habitat it blooms between July and December producing [[inflorescence]]s that appear in groups of two to eight on an axillary raceme. The spherical flower heads have a diameter of {{cvt|5|to|10|mm}} and contain 30 to 50 densely packed pale yellow to nearly white flowers. Following flowering, smooth, firmly papery and glabrous [[seed pod]]s form. The curved, twisted or coiled pods have a biconvex shape with a length of {{cvt|4|to|12|cm}} and a width of {{cvt|5|to|8|mm}} and contain longitudinally arranged seeds.<ref name=pnet>{{cite web|url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acacia~melanoxylon|title=''Acacia melanoxylon'' R.Br.|work=PlantNet|access-date=12 December 2020|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney]]|archive-date=24 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024002437/https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acacia~melanoxylon|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first formally described by the botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in 1813 as a part of the [[William Aiton]] work ''Hortus Kewensis''. It was reclassified as ''Racosperma melanoxylon'' by [[Leslie Pedley]] in 1986 then returned to genus ''Acacia'' in 2006. Several other synonyms are known including ''Acacia arcuata'', ''Mimosa melanoxylon'' and ''Acacia melanoxylon'' var. ''obtusifolia''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bie.ala.org.au/species/https://id.biodiversity.org.au/node/apni/2903496#names|title=''Acacia melanoxylon'' R.Br.|access-date=12 December 2020|work=Atlas of Living Australia|publisher=[[Global Biodiversity Information Facility]]|archive-date=13 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200413053901/https://bie.ala.org.au/species/https://id.biodiversity.org.au/node/apni/2903496#names|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Distribution==
In its native range, ''A. melanoxylon'' is found down the east coast of [[Australia]] from [[Queensland]] in the north, into [[New South Wales]], through [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and west along the south coast of [[South Australia]]. It is also found along the east coast of [[Tasmania]]. It has become naturalised in [[Western Australia]]. In New South Wales it is widespread from coastal areas and into the [[Great Dividing Range]] but is not found further inland. It is commonly found at higher altitudes in the Nandewar Range, Liverpool Range and around [[Orange, New South Wales|Orange]] in the west. It is mostly found as a part of wet [[sclerophyll]] forest communities or near cooler rainforest communities.<ref name=pnet/> The range of the tree extends from the [[Atherton Tableland]] in northern Queensland and follows the coast to around the [[Mount Lofty Range]] in South Australia and can grow in a wide range of [[podsol]]s, especially in sandy loams.<ref name=www/>

==Timber==
''A. melanoxylon'' is valued for its decorative timber which may be used in cabinets, musical instruments and in boatbuilding.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=2024 |title=Blackwood |url=https://www.woodsolutions.com.au/wood-species/hardwood/blackwood |url-status=live |access-date=10 November 2025 |website=Wood Solutions |publisher=Forest and Wood Products Australia Ltd |archive-date=15 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251115180525/https://www.woodsolutions.com.au/wood-species/hardwood/blackwood }}</ref>

===Appearance===
Sapwood may range in colour from straw to grey-white with clear demarcation from the heartwood. The heartwood is golden to dark brown with chocolate growth rings. The timber is generally straight grained but may be wavy or interlocked. Quartersawn surfaces may produce an attractive fiddleback figure. The wood is lustrous and possesses a fine to medium texture.<ref>{{cite book | last = Porter | first = Terry | title = Wood: Identification and Use | publisher = Guild of Master Craftsman Publications Ltd | location = East Sussex, GB | year = 2006 | pages = 37}}</ref>

The name of the wood may refer to dark stains on the hands of woodworkers, caused by the high levels of [[tannin]] in the timber.<ref name=":1" />

===Properties===
''A. melanoxylon'' timber - commonly known as "blackwood" -  has a density of approximately 660 kg/m<sup>3</sup> and is strong in compression, resistant to impact and is moderately stiff. It is moderately blunting to work with tools and bends well. It may be nailed or screwed with ease, but gluing may produce variable results. The wood is easily stained and produces a high-quality finish.<ref name=":1" />

Australian blackwood seasons easily with some possible cupping when boards are inadequately restrained. The timber produces little movement once seasoned.

The timber is susceptible to attacks by furniture beetles, termites and powder-post beetles (sapwood) due to its physical resistance to effective preservative treatments.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

The timber provides very high [[Chatoyancy|chatoyance]], with an average value above 26 PZC.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Australian Blackwood |url=https://www.chatometry.com/australian-blackwood/ |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=PZC Chatometry |language=it-IT}}</ref>

== Invasive species ==
The species has been introduced to many countries for forestry plantings and as an ornamental tree. It now is present in Africa, Asia, Europe, Indian Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, South America and the United States. It is a declared [[noxious weed]] species in South Africa and is a pest in Portugal's [[Azores]] Islands.  It was also recently listed by the [[California Invasive Plant Council]] (Cal-IPC) as an invasive weed that may cause limited impact (Knapp 2003). Its use as a street tree is being phased out in some locales because of the damage it often causes to pavements and underground plumbing. In some regions of Tasmania, blackwood is now considered a pest.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

== Uses ==
[[Indigenous Australians]] use many parts of ''A. melanoxylon'' for a variety of purposes.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Ngunnawal Elders |title=Ngunnawal Plant Use |publisher=ACT Government |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-921117-15-2 |edition=2nd |pages=13 |language=en}}</ref> Seeds are harvested and consumed as a common [[bush tucker]] food, and leaves can be used as a [[soap]] or fishing poison.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=A. Melanoxylon |url=http://users.lycaeum.org/~mulga/acacia/melano.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070527022431/http://users.lycaeum.org/~mulga/acacia/melano.html |archive-date=2007-05-27 |access-date=2007-06-19}}</ref> The bark is either harvested to make string or prepared as a traditional [[analgesic]],<ref name=":0" /><ref>[http://www.newcrops.uq.edu.au/newslett/ncnl1020.htm Analgesic Plants] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070423092423/http://www.newcrops.uq.edu.au/newslett/ncnl1020.htm |date=April 23, 2007 }} Australian New Crops Newsletter</ref> while wood is often used to make [[Clapstick|clap sticks]], [[Woomera (spear-thrower)|spear-throwers]] and [[shield]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/gardens/education/programs/pdfs/aboriginal_plant_use_and_technology.pdf|title=Aboriginal Plant use and Technology|access-date=11 November 2016|publisher=Australian National Botanic Garden|archive-date=27 January 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170127223958/http://www.anbg.gov.au/gardens/education/programs/pdfs/aboriginal_plant_use_and_technology.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> 

The live plant is also employed as a fire barrier in rural settings when grown amongst other fire-resistant species.

Blackwood timber is commercially milled for wood paneling, furniture, joinery and cabinetry, tool handles, boat-building, inlaid boxes and wooden kegs. It is often qualitatively compared to walnut hardwood, and its physical properties are well-suited for shaping with steam. The bark contains a [[tannin]] content of about 20%,<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=CfDcl2m-6BMC&dq=%22acacia+longifolia%22+uses&pg=PA8 Google Books] ''Select Extra-tropical Plants Readily Eligible for Industrial Culture Or Naturalization'' By Ferdinand von Mueller</ref> and is often engineered to produce decorative wood [[Wood veneer|veneer]].<ref name=":1" /> Plain and figured Australian blackwood is used for musical instruments; in particular, guitars, drums, Hawaiian ukuleles, violin bows and organ pipes. More recently, blackwood has seen an increasing value as a substitute for [[Acacia koa|koa]] wood.
